summary: Surveys a range of authentication technologies and gives protocol designers suggestions about which kinds fit which protocols and applications on the Internet. It is informational guidance, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A guide to the different ways a computer can check you are really you, and which way fits which job.

questions: how to choose authentication for a protocol
subtitle: A 1994 tour of authentication technologies, from plain passwords to public keys, and which ones suit which Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: Authentication needs vary widely, yet many Internet protocols relied on passwords that eavesdroppers can capture and replay.
tldr.mechanism: The memo classifies authentication by the attacks it resists, explains symmetric and asymmetric cryptography, checksums and signatures, and discusses user-to-host and service authentication and key management.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that strong cryptographic authentication is needed soon, that public key technology should be used when practical, and that mechanisms vulnerable to passive attack should be phased out.

today: RFC 1704 is an Informational memo from October 1994 and does not specify a standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so read its 1994 recommendations as a historical snapshot.

sections.title: Why Passwords Are Not Enough
sections.content:
Authentication needs differ with a system's use, accessibility and connectivity. This memo describes a spectrum of authentication technologies and gives protocol developers suggestions about which kinds may suit which protocols and applications.

The authors say passwords, which are vulnerable to passive attack, are not strong enough for the current Internet, and that passive and active attacks are not uncommon. They believe many protocols should at least be protected from passive attacks, and that protection against active attack is clearly desirable. Designers should weigh whether authentication is machine to machine or human to machine, local or distributed, how strong it is and how keys are managed.

The memo defines its terms for this document only. A passive attack only watches traffic, an active attack inserts or modifies packets, and a replay attack records and resends valid messages, which works against any constant authentication information such as a password. Symmetric cryptography uses one key for both encryption and decryption; asymmetric cryptography uses two mathematically related keys and is also called public key cryptography.
sections.plainLanguage: A plain password is like shouting your secret across a crowded room. Anyone listening can use it, so many things need something better.

sections.title: A Spectrum of Authentication
sections.content:
The memo orders mechanisms by what they withstand, while noting this is not a strict hierarchy.

  • None: acceptable for a non-networked PC in a secure location or a public workstation with non-sensitive data.
  • Vulnerable to passive attack: simple, disclosing passwords or keys that are exposed if sent over a network, and open to replay.
  • Vulnerable to active attack: non-disclosing schemes. The memo names the SecurID Card (synchronized clocks), S/Key (many single-use passwords from one secret, but open to dictionary attack on a poor pass phrase) and challenge-response systems such as the PPP CHAP, which is non-disclosing but only useful locally.
  • Not vulnerable to active attack: cryptographic systems that use both parties' computing power, may be mutual, and set up a shared session key, for example through a ticket.
sections.plainLanguage: Some checks are like a password anyone can overhear. Better ones change every time, like a code that works only once. The best ones also stop someone sneaking fake messages in.

sections.title: Cryptographic Tools
sections.content:
Symmetric systems need keys delivered securely, by courier or by a key distribution protocol such as Needham and Schroeder's. The memo describes Kerberos, built on DES, where a trusted third-party host knows every user's and service's secret key, so it must be physically secure. If a user's password leaks, an attacker can masquerade as that user anywhere that trusts the Kerberos server.

Asymmetric systems use different keys to encrypt and decrypt, which greatly simplifies key distribution. RSA is the best known, and SPX is an experimental system that uses RSA and a hierarchy of certifying authorities in place of Kerberos's key distribution center.

Cryptographic checksums give integrity and authentication but not non-repudiation. Secure SNMP and SNMPv2 compute an MD5 checksum over a shared secret and the data. Digital signatures with public keys can also prove origin even if the sender denies it, which is called non-repudiation.
sections.plainLanguage: With one shared key, both people hold the same secret. With a public-and-private pair, anyone can lock a box but only the owner can open it. A signature is like a stamp only you can make.

sections.title: Authenticating Users to Hosts
sections.content:
Most systems of the time sent plain-text disclosing passwords over telnet or rlogin, which gives no protection from replay. The memo says failing to use at least a non-disclosing password system effectively grants access to anyone who can reach the network, for example the Ethernet cable, and calls that unacceptable in an Internet. A non-disclosing password system is the minimal defense against eavesdropping and still works from a dumb terminal.

Perimeter defenses, where users authenticate first to a firewall host, are called a short-term tool. Their drawbacks include that the gateway must treat each service independently, double authentication is hard for computer-to-computer traffic, and the perimeter must be tight because the inside is weak if it breaks.

For active attacks, the memo points to session encryption such as Kerberos, or to replay-resistant mechanisms using time stamps, possibly with NTPv3 for synchronized clocks. Another option is for remotely accessible workstations to publish a public key, so users encrypt a password to it, with the limit that this authenticates workstations, not individual users.
sections.plainLanguage: Typing a plain password over the network is like reading it out loud in a hallway. Using codes that change each time, or locking the message so only the right computer can open it, keeps eavesdroppers out.

sections.title: Key Distribution and Management
sections.content:
The memo calls key management perhaps the hardest problem in authentication across large internetworks. The Needham and Schroeder protocol used by Kerberos relies on a central key server, so a large internetwork needs at least one per administrative domain and a way for them to cooperate.

Public key algorithms are expensive for bulk encryption but useful for setting up and exchanging symmetric session keys, and they can remove the central key server. RSA and Diffie-Hellman can both be used. Key certificates, where a trusted authority signs a public key, could be distributed through directory services, for instance a new DNS record type. Multicast key management scales poorly, because the number of exchanges grows with the number of parties.

Published key management protocols have a long history of subtle flaws, so the memo says it is desirable to keep key management separate from authentication or encryption mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Keys are only useful if the right people get them safely. Handing out keys to everyone is the hardest part, and even clever plans have had hidden holes.

sections.title: Services and Future Directions
sections.content:
For host-to-host protocols, the memo notes that most had no authentication, and that original SNMP and some routing protocols used disclosing passwords as a transitional aid. Secure SNMP added optional authentication with an MD5 checksum over a shared secret, and optional DES confidentiality. Where both are needed, session encryption may use symmetric keys, asymmetric keys or both, and Privacy Enhanced Mail shows user-to-user security built into the application.

Looking ahead, the authors expect non-disclosing systems soon and wider public key use later. They note that a public key cannot be memorized, so users may carry private keys in a smart card. They conclude that strong cryptographic authentication is needed in the near future, public key technology should be used when practical and cost-effective, mechanisms vulnerable to passive attack should be phased out, and more research is needed on key management and scalable multicast security.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors think computers will move to stronger secret-keeping over time, and people may carry a small card holding a key too long to remember.
